newsitem.title: USA: INSTANT VIEW - U.S. GDP grew by 5.6 percent in Q1.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW - U.S. GDP grew by 5.6 percent in Q1.

text.p: Following are comments from U.S. economists after the Commerce Department reported real Gross Domestic Product (GDP) grew at an annual rate of 5.6 percent in the first quarter of 1997, a nine-year high, after an increase of 3.8 percent in the final estimate of the fourth quarter 1996. Economists in a Reuters survey had expected, on average, a 4.1 percent rise in the first quarter.
IRWIN KELLNER, KELLNER ECONOMIC ADVISERS: "These numbers appear to be for another country; they just don't square with any of the monthly numbers we've seen."
Kellner was speaking on Reuters Financial Television.

KEVIN FLANAGAN, VICE PRESIDENT AND MONEY MARKET ECONOMIST, DEAN WITTER REYNOLDS INC: "This is telling us the economy's just roaring ahead. This is a bout of momentum going forward into the April to June period, and it's bound to catch the (Federal Reserve's) attention."

JOSEPH DZIWURA, VICE PRESIDENT AND AN ECONOMIST, SAKURA BANK: "It looks like (the report's strength) is all in the consumer sector. Gross domestic purchases -- GDP minus inventories and net exports -- were up 7.3 percent, so domestic consumption is just explosive.
"Gross domestic purchases in the fourth quarter were only 1.6 (percent). With this number, it looks like we've got momentum going forward ... that the Fed's likely to move again."

RICHARD BERNER, CHIEF ECONOMIST, MELLON BANK CORP: "Obviously, these data are strong across the board. There was a big surprise in inventories and to some extent that depends on what you assume for March."

Berner continued: "I think it still means what it meant before. The Fed is on track to tighten again in May. What (Fed Governor) Larry Meyer said last week is still operative, namely that inflation looks very much under control right now. The basic point is this kind of persistent strength in the economy and tight labor markets put upward pressure on prices and the Fed wants to keep that under control."
JOSH STILES, SENIOR BOND STRATEGIST, I.D.E.A. INC: "The data highlight the Fed's dilemma. They show very strong growth but no disturbing inflation.

"The main upside surprise is in inventories. Also, raising eyebrows was the deflator ticking up to 2.3 percent. The market was looking for a deflator number slightly under 2.0 percent. Personal consumption we knew was strong, but it was even stronger than expected -- at 6.4 percent. Otherwise, the components are pretty much as expected. It's a very strong number and to me, it's a little surprising that the bond market is only off a quarter point.

Stiles continued: "The reaction to the data is not that big yet. I would not expect a move to 110 (on the June bond contract) until we get the April payroll data on Friday. I would lower my sights for any upside potential ahead of the payroll number."

ETHAN HARRIS, SENIOR ECONOMIST, LEHMAN GOVERNMENTS SECURITIES INC: "Obviously, this was a blowout number ... It keeps the Fed very nervous. The only silver lining was that all of the surprise was in inventories, which grew $20 billion more than consensus.
"But this will get people to revise down GDP growth in the second quarter. We'll get about a 1.0 percent drag from inventories alone in the second quarter."
